extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in sociology, criminology, media studies and social policy
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying and interpreting public and private letters, press correspondence, and informal communications to understand how public opinion about crime is formed and structured in a local case. Emphasises typologies of letter-writers, rhetorical features, ideological repertoires, and channels of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental / sociological explanation (the 'environmentalist' case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is explained by social, emotional, economic or educational under-privilege originating in history (slums, poverty, unemployment); social scientists can give 'fairly sound guesses' as to how these factors affect individual behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters adopting this perspective invoke structural causes and the social environment; often authored by welfare-state professionals (prison psychologist, social worker, probation officer). Use this criterion to identify correspondents who locate crime in context and argue for social remedies rather than purely punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditionalist / moral-discipline explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is opposed as a product of individual moral failure; respectability, self-discipline and 'lifting oneself by one's moral bootstraps' overcome environmental disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for appeals to personal experience, common-sense realism, and recommendations for moral/social institutions (Guides, Scouts, Boys' Brigade, youth clubs, church/school). These letters emphasise individual responsibility and social/moral discipline as solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private vs public channel distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes 'letters to the editor' (public, citizen-to-citizen discourse) from private abusive letters (person-to-person, often anonymous) that would be unacceptable in public taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form (public address vs personal/private), intended audience, anonymity, tone and conventions to assign channel. Note that private letters may nonetheless draw on and amplify public ideologies; channel alone does not imply separate underlying attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abusive letters as transformation of public attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Abusive private letters express more extreme language or suggestions but are often transformations (formal intensifications) of attitudes present in public correspondence; authors assume an 'invisible public' that largely agrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify abusive letters by extreme tone, personal address, anonymity and violent imagery; treat them as a register of intensified public sentiment rather than purely irrational outliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retributivist letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers demand that the law must exact retribution; moralizing chain 'bad-wickedness-deserves-blame' is prevalent. Advocates of corporal punishment or extended sentences typically remain within what the text calls 'acceptable extremism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify letters as retributivist when focus is on victim's suffering and proportional punitive response (life sentences, corporal punishment) rather than extra-legal violence or total dehumanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revengist / super-retributivist letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely abusive correspondence that contains brutal punishment recommendations (lynching, sterilisation, sadistic methods) and dehumanizing labels ('vermin', 'animal', 'scum'). Often incorporates racist-sexual themes and explicit calls for vengeance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag letters with calls for extrajudicial violence, exterminatory language, or racialized/sexualized scapegoating as super-retributivist; these mark the furthest end of the abusive spectrum and indicate authoritarian/authoritarian-personality structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal testimony / 'personal-expert' experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters that mobilise personal victimisation or professional identity (prison officer's wife, grandson of a magistrates' chairman, father of an attacked son) to legitimise views and rebut alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat first-person anecdote and stated credentials as rhetorical devices that confer authority; distinguish between anecdotal counter-evidence and systemic evidence when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring ideological 'root-concepts' (family, race, sexuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Core images underlie many letters: centrality of the family ('normal' family produces 'normal' children), race (alien/native distinctions, welfare-state tropes), and sexuality (accusations of promiscuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing letters, map references to these root-concepts as organizing metaphors that connect disparate arguments and reveal deeper normative commitments and stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process of public opinion formation (channels and stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion progresses from informal local talk (conversations, gossip, street-corners, pubs) to local press (letters to the editor), to media amplification (news, features, editorials) and back into the public domain; as issues become more public they are increasingly structured by available ideologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess an issue's movement through these stages and the corresponding shifts in framing and constraints. Use this sequence to explain how local meanings are reworked into nationally legible 'public issues'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/ source inflection of discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Different institutional actors (police, courts, social workers, local experts, different newspapers) speak in distinct idioms and shape interpretations according to their professional worlds; courts produce judicial reasoning, police the language of containment, social workers a social-care idiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding statements, note the institutional origin and expect characteristic frames; analyse how the interaction of sources (courts + media) anchors 'dominant interpretations'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological lexicon / recurrent premises
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring repertoire of premises and labels (e.g., 'layabout' = unemployed = scrounger = bad; 'what about the victim?'; 'cost' and 'payment') structures many letters across channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify these lexical markers as shorthand for broader ideological positions; they help trace continuity across differently framed texts and registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal textual features as indicators of stance and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface features—length (critical letters often longer), tone, formatting (capital letters, headings, spacing), attachments (photographs), signatures/addresses—signal effort, obsession, seriousness, or attempts to 'make an impact'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these formal markers to infer the writer's investment, performative intent, and whether a letter is designed to sway, intimidate, or mobilise. Longer, formatted, or materially augmented letters often indicate more elaborated argumentation or obsession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and 'refusal of sociality' as measures of abusive communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal abusive letters are frequently anonymous and decline reciprocity (no expectation of dialogue), producing menace; anonymity combined with direct address intensifies abusiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify anonymous, directly abusive, non-reciprocal letters as carrying a higher threat-level. Consider anonymity as a structural feature that both enables extreme language and signals a withdrawal from social norms of exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing 'acceptable extremism' from 'lunatic fringe'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some extreme recommendations (e.g., corporal punishment, long sentences) remain within a socially acceptable range, while others are dismissed as 'cranks' or 'lunatic fringe'; the boundary is porous and culturally mediated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating extremity, situate proposals relative to contemporary judicial/political possibilities and public tolerances; treat the distinction as analytical rather than absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime-as-archetype framing (victim-centred moral outrage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The press depiction of a crime (merciless, gratuitous violence against an innocent) provides an archetype that legitimates moral outrage and retributive responses among letter-writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how media portrayals supply premises for public letters: the 'archetypal violent criminal' image becomes a premise justifying harsh punishment and moral condemnation in subsequent public discourse.
